overview: I2202 builds the geometry that makes radio navigation usable when the clearance is not simply direct-to or radial tracking. Be ready to compute arc lead points, leave an arc on time, solve point-to-point headings, and handle oxygen-system or physiological problems without losing the instrument scan.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Arcing is flying at a constant DME from a NAVAID. You approximate the arc with small heading and bank changes; you are not trying to draw a perfect circle.

children.text: Proceed direct to the arc entry point defined by radial and DME.
Calculate the lead point, determine the turn direction, and begin a standard-rate turn at the lead point.
Continue the turn until the bearing-pointer head is on the 90-degree benchmark for the arc direction.
Check DME immediately after rollout and correct early instead of waiting for a large displacement.
In no wind, bearing-pointer head on the 90-degree benchmark means DME is constant.
Bearing-pointer head below the 90-degree benchmark means DME is increasing.
Bearing-pointer head above the 90-degree benchmark means DME is decreasing.
If inside the arc, maintain heading or place the bearing-pointer head up to 15 degrees below the benchmark; if outside, place it up to 15 degrees above the benchmark.
Common errors are late lead-point planning, turning the wrong direction, and overcorrecting DME instead of making small benchmark changes.

items.text: A radial-arc intercept transitions from tracking a radial to joining an arc at a specified DME.

children.text: For a standard-rate 90-degree turn, turn radius is 0.5% of groundspeed in NM; for example, 150 knots is about 0.75 NM.
If groundspeed is not available in time, KIAS may be used as a no-wind approximation.
When a full standard-rate turn is not appropriate, use 1.0% of groundspeed for a half-standard-rate lead point.
Apply the turn radius so the aircraft begins turning before the arc DME, then adjust for known wind.
Start the turn at the computed DME and roll toward the 90-degree bearing-pointer benchmark.
Check whether the first DME trend puts you inside or outside the arc, then correct with the arcing benchmark logic.
The briefing-guide emphasis is to know turn direction from the assigned arc direction before reaching the lead point.

items.text: An arc-radial intercept leaves an arc and joins an inbound or outbound radial. The key is calculating the lead radial early enough that the turn finishes on course.

children.text: Find radials per NM with the 60-to-1 rule: 60 divided by arc DME.
Find turn radius: 0.5% of groundspeed for standard-rate, or 1.0% for half-standard-rate.
Multiply turn radius by radials per NM; that product is the no-wind lead radial.
Set the CDI for the course you will intercept before reaching the lead radial, then begin the turn at the lead radial.
Greater arc DME means fewer lead radials because radials are farther apart.
Half-standard-rate turns need more lead radials than standard-rate turns because the turn takes longer.
Adjust the no-wind lead for known wind, then track the new radial or course after rollout.

items.text: An OBOGS malfunction is a crew-survival problem before it is a system-analysis problem. Keep flying, get a secure oxygen source, descend when required, and use the checklist.

children.text: An OBOGS FAIL warning can indicate low bleed-air pressure, low oxygen concentration, or an internal failure detected by the system.
OBOGS TEMP indicates a heat-exchanger failure and is treated as an OBOGS failure.
Physiological symptoms or zeolite-dust indications can occur without a warning light; coughing, respiratory irritation, or white dust in the mask still demand immediate action.
Engine failure, total electrical failure, main battery depletion, or battery failure removes OBOGS support.
Check both cockpits: supply ON, concentration MAX, pressure EMERGENCY, flow indication, hose/CRU-60/P connection, and mask seal.
If symptoms are recognized, immediately execute the OBOGS Failure/Overtemp/Physiological Symptoms procedure instead of troubleshooting first.
Emergency oxygen provides about 10 minutes; above 10,000 feet cockpit altitude, pulling the green ring is required before depletion risk becomes incapacitating.
Initiate descent below 10,000 feet MSL, secure OBOGS supply OFF as directed, and land as soon as practical.

items.text: Hypoxia and hyperventilation can feel similar early, so the safe cockpit answer is to protect oxygen first, then normalize breathing once the oxygen source is secure.

children.text: Hypoxia is oxygen deficiency in body tissues; early signs can include poor judgment, euphoria, fatigue, tunnel vision, dizziness, or headache.
Advanced hypoxia can progress to cyanosis, confusion, loss of coordination, unconsciousness, and incapacitation.
Susceptibility increases with factors such as fatigue, dehydration, illness, alcohol, medication, smoking, carbon monoxide exposure, temperature stress, and exertion.
Hyperventilation is abnormally rapid or deep breathing that lowers carbon dioxide.
Symptoms can include lightheadedness, tingling, drowsiness, muscle spasms, a feeling of suffocation, and in severe cases unconsciousness.
When breathing oxygen under increased pressure, breathe slightly slower and shallower than normal to avoid inducing hyperventilation.
If unsure which one you have, treat it like hypoxia first: secure oxygen, verify flow, descend as required, tell the other cockpit, then consciously slow and normalize breathing.
Do not let symptom analysis pull both pilots heads-down; keep one pilot flying and scanning.

items.text: Point-to-point navigation uses a VOR/DME or VORTAC to fly directly from present position to a radial/DME fix without waiting for radar vectors.

children.text: Tune, identify, and monitor the NAVAID.
Set the desired radial in the CDI; this helps build the picture even when it is not the heading you will fly.
Visualize the station at the center of the HSI compass card.
Plot the fix with the greater DME on the edge of the compass card and the smaller-DME fix proportionally closer to center.
Turn initially to a heading between the bearing-pointer head and the course-pointer head: split the heads.
Favor the bearing-pointer head when going to a smaller DME; favor the course-pointer head when going to a larger DME.
Use the pencil method to draw the present-position-to-desired-fix line, move that line to the center of the card, and read the updated no-wind heading.
Keep updating en route. If the line tilts right, turn right; if it tilts left, turn left.
As you near the fix, compare DME rate to radial-crossing rate.
If arriving at DME first, use the 90-degree benchmark to split the bearing pointer and desired radial; do not arc to the radial.
If arriving at the radial first, turn to track inbound or outbound as required toward the fix.
Common errors are delaying the initial turn, splitting the wrong heads, using the reciprocal radial, failing to update the pencil solution, and trying to arc to the fix.

studyNotes.summary: Lead the arc, manage DME with bearing-pointer benchmarks, solve point-to-point geometry early, and treat oxygen or physiological symptoms as immediate crew-survival problems.

summary: Arcing, arc intercept math, point-to-point navigation, and oxygen/physiology emergency priorities.
title: Arcing and Radial Intercepts
